extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for USPTO examiners on analyzing whether claimed inventions meet 35 U.S.C. §101 (statutory categories and judicial-exception/Alice–Mayo analysis), including claim construction, flowchart pathways, and how to formulate rejections and responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two criteria for subject matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention must (1) be to one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) and (2) qualify as patent-eligible subject matter — i.e., the claim must not be directed to a judicial exception unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the overarching two-part requirement. The MPEP references the Alice/Mayo two‑part test for the second criterion and MPEP §2106.03 for the four categories. See cited Supreme Court cases (Alice, Mayo, Diehr, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category requirement (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter as enumerated by 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-process categories, the claimed invention must exist in some physical or tangible form. See detailed definitions: process = actions/series of acts; machine = concrete thing of parts/devices; manufacture = tangible article given new form/quality; composition = combination of two or more substances. If a claim does not fall within any category, reject under §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-statutory product examples (Step 1 anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of claims that do not fall within the statutory categories: information/data per se; computer program per se (software per se) when claimed without structural recitations; transitory propagating electrical/electromagnetic signals (signals per se); subject matter expressly prohibited (e.g., humans per se).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These serve as concrete non-statutory examples when evaluating whether a product claim has physical/tangible form. Even if created by human effort, an intangible collection of information or code detached from a medium is not a statutory product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) must be established first
rubrics_metrics.description: Before analyzing eligibility, establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI sets claim boundaries and influences whether the claim falls within statutory categories or encompasses judicial exceptions. Claim construction can change the result (see Mentor Graphics, Enfish, Synopsys examples). See MPEP §2111 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI covering both statutory and non-statutory embodiments => Step 1 failure
rubrics_metrics.description: If the BRI of the claim covers both statutory and non‑statutory embodiments, the claim embraces non-statutory subject matter and fails Step 1 (not to a statutory category).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When this occurs, a §101 rejection is appropriate; examiners should point out the BRI and recommend amendments narrowing the claim to statutory embodiments where possible (best practice). Example: machine‑readable medium that can cover carrier waves (non-stat.) and memory (stat.). Use form paragraphs 7.05/7.05.01 per MPEP §2106.07(a)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-part test (Step 2 overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim passes Step 1, apply the Alice/Mayo two-part test: Step 2A — determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon); Step 2B — if so, determine whether additional claim elements individually or as an ordered combination amount to significantly more than the exception (i.e., an 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two‑part test is the controlling framework. The flowchart organizes analysis into Pathways A (self-evident eligibility), B (not directed to judicial exception), and C (directed to exception but amounts to significantly more).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — Identify judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, a law of nature, or a natural phenomenon (judicial exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract ideas include mathematical formulas, certain methods of organizing human activity, mental processes, etc. Use the MPEP discussion and listed groupings/examples. Claims directed to nothing more than these exceptions are not patent eligible absent 'integration' or 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A prong two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim integrates the judicial exception into a practical application such that the claim is not 'directed to' the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integration factors include whether the claim uses the exception in a manner that applies it in a practical way (e.g., improves computer functionality, applies a particular treatment). If integrated into a practical application, the claim may be eligible at Step 2A (Pathway B) without reaching Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating improvements in the functioning of a computer or other technology (Step 2A/2B indicia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claim improves the functioning of a computer or another technology or technical field, which supports eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts (e.g., Enfish, McRO) found claims eligible where the claim language tied the exception to unconventional technical solutions or rules that improved existing technological processes. Such improvements can show the claim is not directed to an abstract idea or that it provides 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — 'Amounting to significantly more' / inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, evaluate whether additional elements individually or in combination add 'significantly more' than the exception (the 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for meaningful limitations beyond the exception: unconventional technical features, particular machine or transformation, or other improvements to technology. The second part is the 'search for an inventive concept' as described in Alice and Mayo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular machine indicator (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim element that ties the exception to a particular machine may indicate 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The machine-or-transformation test is a relevant clue but not a separate test; reliance on a generic computer or special-purpose computer is insufficient by itself. The claimed machine must meaningfully limit the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular transformation indicator (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting a particular transformation of an article into a different state or thing can indicate patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transformation must be meaningful (not merely insignificant data manipulation or token activity). Particular transformation remains a relevant clue under Step 2B (related to the machine-or-transformation concept).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity is insufficient (Step 2B negative indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting well-understood, routine, conventional steps or components that are known in the art does not make a claim that is directed to a judicial exception eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements are merely generic or conventional implementation of the exception, they do not supply the required 'significantly more.' See MPEP §2106.05(d) and related case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception and insignificant extra-solution activity are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that are nothing more than instructions to apply an abstract idea, or that add insignificant extra-solution activity, do not make the claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include steps like 'apply the formula' or adding conventional post‑solution activity (e.g., data gathering, storing) that do not add a meaningful inventive concept. See MPEP §2106.05(f) and §2106.05(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-of-use and technological environment limitations are not sufficient by themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply limiting an abstract idea to a particular field of use or technological environment (e.g., the Internet) does not render the claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims cannot be made non-abstract merely by restricting their application to a particular technological field or environment. See cited cases (Intellectual Ventures, TLI Communications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test is a useful clue, not a separate test
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation test may inform the analysis but should not be applied as an independent eligibility test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the test as part of the integration/significantly-more determinations under Alice/Mayo; do not treat machine-or-transformation as dispositive on its own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis (Pathway A) for self-evident eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim's eligibility is self-evident (or clearly shows improvement in technology/computer functionality), examiners may use a streamlined analysis and find the claim eligible at Pathway A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If uncertain about streamlined analysis appropriateness, conduct full eligibility analysis. Pathway A saves examiner effort for claims where eligibility is evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathways B and C definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathway B: claim falls within a statutory category and is not directed to a judicial exception (Step2A:NO) — eligible. Pathway C: claim falls within a statutory category, is directed to a judicial exception (Step2A:YES), but recites additional elements that amount to significantly more (Step2B:YES) — eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim does not qualify under any pathway (A, B, or C), it is ineligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not evaluate eligibility based on 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' or on utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility should not be judged based on whether the claim recites a 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' or on the utility of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier tests (e.g., State Street 'useful, concrete, and tangible result') have been superseded. Utility under §101 is not the test for subject-matter eligibility; other statutes (35 U.S.C. 112, 102, 103) address those concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay with other statutory requirements (102, 103, 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: Passage of the §101 eligibility threshold does not obviate examination under 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description/enablement/claim definiteness), 102 (novelty), and 103 (non-obviousness); examiners must perform complete examination under all applicable statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §101 is a threshold inquiry. Even if a claim is eligible under §101, it still must satisfy other conditions and requirements of the Patent Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation can affect both Step 1 and Alice/Mayo analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: How claim terms are construed (under BRI and specification) can change whether a claim is statutory or directed to an exception, and whether additional elements provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mentor Graphics (machine-readable medium scope), Synopsys (mental steps), Enfish and McRO (technical improvements). Use specification and claim language consistently when construing claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating and supporting §101 rejections; examiner procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a §101 rejection, use appropriate form paragraphs and explain reasoning; evaluate applicant responses and clarify the record as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP §2106.07 gives guidance on formulating rejections, specific form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05, 7.05.01), evaluating applicant responses, and documenting/clarifying the record. Recommend amendments where appropriate and explain BRI if relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined vs. full analysis best practice
rubrics_metrics.description: If eligibility is self-evident, streamlined analysis may be used; if uncertain, examiners should conduct the full two-part Alice/Mayo analysis to ensure consistent and correct results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that could be eligible under Pathway A but are unclear should be fully analyzed under Steps 2A/2B; this promotes consistency and reduces risk of error.
